subtype: Approach: writing and rehearsing the speech [Action]
passage: Hafsa, you're nervous about tomorrow's speech, so listen to your Baljeet Uncle. At sixteen I stood for house captain. I wrote my speech on the back of a calendar page. One promise: proper drainage so the ground would not flood during monsoon practice. One story: the day my shoes floated away in the middle of a football match. I read it to the mirror every night. Then I read it to my friend Gulshan, who timed me on his watch: three minutes ten. Too long. I cut every "as we all know" and "respected teachers and friends," and got it down to two minutes flat. On the day, the hall laughed at the shoes and remembered the drainage. I won by a small margin, and Gulshan claimed half the credit.

qa.q: What was the one promise in Baljeet's speech?
qa.a: The promise was proper drainage so the ground would not flood during monsoon practice.

qa.q: How might Baljeet have felt while reading to the mirror each night, and what does it show?
qa.a: Baljeet was probably nervous but determined, shown by the nightly practice and the willingness to be timed and corrected.

qa.q: What choice in the story shortened the speech, and why did it help?
qa.a: Cutting the filler phrases brought it to two minutes, because a shorter speech keeps the one promise and the story clear.

qa.q: How did Gulshan help in the story?
qa.a: Gulshan timed the speech on his watch and showed that it was too long at three minutes ten.

grounding: The candidate drafts a two-minute speech with one clear promise and one story, practises before a mirror and a friend, and trims filler after timing it.

Nitin had one evening to prepare his two-minute speech for the class representative election, and the flat was chaos: his cousin's wedding was two days away, and the living room was full of aunties folding saris.

He took his draft to the only quiet place, the building's stairwell. First read-through: three minutes forty. Far too long.

He cut the list of five promises down to one: a proper notice board where every class's test dates were posted. Then he kept one story, about missing a chemistry test because the date changed and nobody told him.

His friend Simran came down with two cups of tea. "Go again. I'll time you." He practised facing the stairwell window like a mirror. Two minutes ten.

"Cut 'basically'," Simran said. "You said it six times." Next run: one minute fifty-five.

qa.q: How long was Nitin's first read-through?
qa.a: His first read-through took three minutes forty.

qa.q: How might Nitin have felt when the first read-through ran far too long?
qa.a: He probably felt frustrated and a bit anxious, with only one evening and a noisy flat to fix it.

qa.q: What else could Nitin practise before the real speech?
qa.a: He could practise once in front of a small group to get used to faces and interruptions, since the stairwell is quieter than a classroom.

qa.q: How does the rehearsal look from Simran's side?
qa.a: Simran seems to enjoy helping and feels useful, timing him and catching the six 'basically's he could not hear himself.

grounding: Shows a candidate, despite a noisy home, drafting a short speech with one promise and one story, practising with a friend and cutting filler after timing.

subtype: Approach: writing and rehearsing the speech [Action]
passage:
Chandrika's speech for school vice-captain began as two full pages. On Sunday afternoon, in the small bedroom of their Chembur flat, she read it aloud to the wardrobe mirror with her phone timer running. Five minutes. The limit was two.

She crossed out every sentence that began with "Also". What remained was one promise: a student helpdesk at the gate every Monday. And one story: the morning a new girl had cried near the gate because she couldn't find her classroom.

Her younger brother Omkar was dragged in as the audience. "Say it without looking," he said. She tried. She forgot the second half.

They ran it four more times. Omkar pointed out she said "like" constantly, so she cut it. By evening she could do it in one minute fifty, looking at him the whole time.

qa.a: Her one promise was a student helpdesk at the gate every Monday.

qa.q: How might Chandrika have felt when she forgot the second half of the speech?
qa.a: She probably felt flustered and a little embarrassed, but determined enough to keep practising.

qa.q: What could Chandrika do if she freezes on the day?
qa.a: She could carry a small card with the promise and the story's key word, so one glance gets her back on track.

qa.q: How might Omkar see his role in the practice?
qa.a: Omkar may feel important and pleased with himself for spotting all the 'like's, even though he was dragged in at first.

grounding: Shows a candidate cutting a long draft to one promise and one story, rehearsing to a mirror and a sibling, and trimming filler after timing.
